name: Barbu
description: Barbu (French for 'The Bearded One', referring to the King of Hearts) is the ultimate compendium card game, a favorite among French bridge players for its strategic depth and psychological complexity. A full session consists of 28 hands, where each of the four players acts as 'Declarer' for 7 hands, choosing from 7 different contracts. The game is a marathon of adaptability, shifting from punishing negative games (where you must avoid specific cards) to high-speed positive games like 'Trump' and the layout-based 'Domino'.

history.origins: Barbu evolved in early 20th-century France from earlier multi-game suites like 'Quodlibet'. In the 1960s, it underwent a resurgence among competitive bridge players, who added the complex 'Doubles' system that turned it into a serious gambling and strategy contest.
timeline: 1910s: Early versions played in French cafes.
1968: The 'Bridge Player's' version with Doubles is standardized.
1980s: Spread to the UK and USA as a high-skill alternative to Hearts.
Present: Widely played in European bridge clubs as a 'relaxed' but still intense side game.
history.cultural: Regarded as a game of 'temporary alliances'; unlike Bridge, you have no permanent partner, but you must constantly negotiate with others to bring down the leader.
history.evolution: The game's name (Barbu) specific focus on the King of Hearts as a 'Bomba' card is shared with Polish Kierki and Middle Eastern Trix.

setup.dealing: Dealer (rotating) deals all cards. Each player receives 13 cards.
setup.equipment: Standard pack, specialized Barbu score sheet (to track 28 rounds).

rules.objective: Accumulate the highest positive score (or lowest negative) at the end of the 28-hand cycle.
rules.gameplay: For all contracts except Domino, standard trick-taking rules apply: must follow suit; highest card of suit led wins the trick (unless trumps are involved).
keyRules: The declarer must play all 7 contracts exactly once during their tenure.
In 'No Hearts', you cannot lead a heart until a heart has been discarded (broken suit).

strategy.basic: In negative rounds, 'dump' your high cards on tricks started by others where no penalties are involved. In Trumps, try to clear your short suits early to use your trumps.
strategy.intermediate: The Double Strategy: If you have a terrible hand for 'No Queens' (e.g., three high Queens), DO NOT double the declarer. If you have an amazing hand for 'No Tricks', double everyoneâ€”you'll harvest their negative points.
strategy.advanced: Void Management: In 'No Barbu', if you realize you are stuck with the Kâ™¥, try to create a 'Void' in another suit so you can discard the King the moment someone else leads that suit.
tips: Domino is the hardest contract to play well. Look for cards that 'Block' your opponents (e.g., holding the 7 of Clubs prevents anyone from starting the bottom or top half of that suit).
Pay attention to what contracts the other players have left. If a player hasn't played 'Trumps' yet and they're low on cards, they will be dangerous.

scoring.description: Total points are tracked across 28 hands. Because points in negative contracts equal points in positive contracts, the total sum of all player scores at the end of the game should be zero.

synthesis.shortDescription: Barbu is the ultimate test of versatility. Across 28 hands, you must dodge Queens, hide from the King of Hearts, dominate in Trumps, and master the intricate blocking of Domino. With the addition of strategic Doubles, every point taken by an opponent can become a victory for you.
